question:
Select the option that contains a grammatical error in the underlined portion.
When Mrs. Sinha came to see Varanasi in 2019, Nupur has already been teaching there for five years.
option_1: When Mrs. Sinha came to see Varanasi __in 2019__, Nupur has already been teaching there for five years.
option_2: __When Mrs. Sinha came to see Varanasi__ in 2019, Nupur has already been teaching there for five years.
option_3: When Mrs. Sinha came to see Varanasi in 2019, Nupur has already been teaching __there for five years__.
option_4: When Mrs. Sinha came to see Varanasi in 2019, __Nupur has already been teaching__ there for five years.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Nupur has already been teaching.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes two actions in the past: Mrs. Sinha's arrival in 2019 (a completed past action) and Nupur's teaching, which had started before that arrival and was still continuing at that point of time.

• Rule — Past Perfect Continuous Tense: When one past action started before another past action and continued up to (or beyond) it, the earlier, continuing action must be expressed in the Past Perfect Continuous Tense: Subject + had been + V1 + ing.
◦ Example: When I reached the station, the train had already been standing there for an hour.

• In the given sentence, "Nupur has already been teaching" wrongly uses the Present Perfect Continuous ("has been teaching"), which is used with a present reference point, not with a past reference point like "When Mrs. Sinha came...". It should be "had already been teaching".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because the underlined portion "in 2019" is grammatically correct; it simply specifies the year of the past action "came".

• Option 2 is incorrect because "When Mrs. Sinha came to see Varanasi" is a correctly formed subordinate clause in the Simple Past Tense.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "there for five years" is a correct adverbial phrase of place and duration; there is no error in it.

NOTE

• Whenever a sentence contains a clause with the Simple Past Tense (e.g., "When... came") describing a point of time, and another action was already in progress before that point, the second action must be in the Past Perfect (Continuous) Tense, never the Present Perfect (Continuous).

• Common signal words for Past Perfect: "already", "before", "by the time", "when...had".

question:
Select the most appropriate idiomatic expression to fill in the blank.
Anita keeps on repeating that she is innocent, but there is ____________.
option_2: no pulling up of the socks
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. no smoke without fire.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "No smoke without fire" means that if there is a rumour or allegation about something, there is usually some truth or basis behind it; rumours rarely arise without at least a grain of truth. (हर अफवाह के पीछे कुछ न कुछ सच्चाई होती है)
◦ Example: He denies taking the money, but there is no smoke without fire — people don't accuse someone without reason.

• Since Anita keeps repeating her innocence but suspicion persists, the idiom fits perfectly — it suggests that the persistent doubt about her probably has some basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "No pulling up of the socks" is not a standard idiom; the correct idiom is "pull up one's socks", meaning to prepare to make more effort.

• Option 3: "No rubbing of the shoulders" is not a standard idiom; the correct idiom is "rub shoulders with", meaning to meet or associate with (especially famous or important) people.

• Option 4: "No love lost between" is an idiom meaning two people/groups dislike each other, which does not fit the context of someone claiming innocence.

NOTE

• Other common idioms with "fire/smoke": "to add fuel to the fire" (to worsen a situation), "to play with fire" (to take a big risk), "fire away" (go ahead and ask/speak).

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.
Those four pages were torn by Jack.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Jack tore those four pages.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "Those four pages were torn by Jack" is in the Passive Voice, Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object

• Applying the rule: the agent "Jack" (after "by") becomes the subject; the past participle "torn" (V3) is converted to the simple past form "tore" (V2); and the subject of the passive sentence, "those four pages", becomes the object, kept unchanged as "those four pages".
◦ Active: Jack tore those four pages.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "tears" is a Simple Present form; the tense of the original passive sentence (Simple Past) must be preserved.

• Option 3 is incorrect on two counts: "tear" is not in the past tense, and the demonstrative "these" wrongly replaces "those".

• Option 4 is incorrect because although the verb "tore" is correctly in the past tense, the demonstrative pronoun has been wrongly changed from "those" to "these".

NOTE

• When converting voice, demonstrative pronouns/adjectives (this/that/these/those) must remain exactly as given — they are never changed.

• V1-V2-V3 for "tear": tear – tore – torn.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
We lived a very frugal life during our childhood.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Extravagant.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Frugal" means economical or sparing in the use of money or resources; thrifty. (मितव्ययी / कम खर्च करने वाला)
◦ Example: Despite being wealthy, she led a frugal life and avoided unnecessary expenses.

• "Extravagant" means spending much more money or resources than is necessary or wise; lavish, which is the exact opposite of "frugal". (फिजूलखर्च)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Reckless" means careless or heedless of consequences — related to carelessness in general, not specifically to spending, so it is not the precise opposite of "frugal".

• Option 2: "Weary" means tired or exhausted; it is unrelated in meaning to "frugal".

• Option 3: "Severe" means harsh or strict; it does not relate to spending habits and so cannot be the antonym of "frugal".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "frugal": thrifty, economical, sparing, prudent.

• Other common antonym pairs tested by SSC: stingy × generous, miserly × lavish, thrifty × wasteful.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
Which cannot be read.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Illegible.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Illegible" is the one-word substitute for "which cannot be read", i.e., writing or print that is not clear enough to be read. (जो पढ़ा न जा सके / अस्पष्ट)
◦ Example: The doctor's handwriting was so illegible that the pharmacist could not read the prescription.

• The word is formed from the negative prefix "il-" + "legible" (able to be read clearly).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Illiterate" means a person who cannot read or write at all — it describes a person's inability, not a piece of writing that is hard to read.

• Option 2: "Inaudible" means that which cannot be heard, relating to sound, not to written text.

• Option 3: "Invisible" means that which cannot be seen at all, which is different from something that exists but is hard to read.

NOTE

• Commonly confused one-word substitutes: Illegible (cannot be read, of handwriting/print) vs Illiterate (a person who cannot read/write) vs Unreadable (too boring/badly written to be read, though technically legible).

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Prefferance.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word is INCORRECTLY spelt in Option 1; the correct spelling is "Preference" — meaning a greater liking for one thing over another.
◦ Example: My preference is to travel by train rather than by bus.

• Spelling key: PRE + FER + ENCE — a single "f" and a single "r" before "-ence"; there is no double "f" and no "a" before "-nce".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Preservation" is correctly spelt — the act of keeping something safe or in its original state.

• Option 3: "Preponderance" is correctly spelt — a superiority in number, quantity, or importance.

• Option 4: "Perseverance" is correctly spelt — continued effort to achieve something despite difficulty.

NOTE

• Related word forms: prefer (verb), preferable (adjective), preferably (adverb) — all keep the single "f" and single "r" pattern.

• Other commonly misspelt "-ence/-ance" words tested by SSC: occurrence, existence, maintenance, appearance, resemblance.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word to fill in the blank.
While most friends persuaded him to choose the career, there were a few who __________ him from doing so.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. dissuaded.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Persuaded" means to convince someone to do something through reasoning or argument. (मनाना / राज़ी करना)

• "Dissuaded" means to convince someone NOT to do something; to discourage someone from a course of action, which is the exact opposite of "persuaded". (हतोत्साहित करना / मना करना)
◦ Example: His friends dissuaded him from investing all his savings in the risky venture.

• The sentence contrasts two groups of friends — those who "persuaded" him one way and a few who did the opposite — so the blank must carry the antonym of "persuaded".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Evaded" means to avoid or escape from something; it does not mean to discourage someone from a decision.

• Option 2: "Bombarded" means to attack persistently (with questions, missiles, etc.); it does not fit the sense of discouraging someone.

• Option 4: "Situated" means located or positioned somewhere; it is unrelated in meaning to "persuaded".

NOTE

• Word family: dissuade (verb) → dissuasion (noun) → dissuasive (adjective).

• Commonly confused pair: persuade (to convince to do) vs dissuade (to convince not to do) — both take the pattern "persuade/dissuade someone from doing something".

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Shakuntala Devi was born on 4th November 1929. In her childhood she ________to school.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. had never been.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence talks about Shakuntala Devi's childhood, a period completed before the time of writing/speaking, so the action needs a past tense form, and since it describes something that did NOT happen throughout that earlier period, the Past Perfect Tense is required.

• Rule — Past Perfect Tense (negative, with "never"): Subject + had + never + V3, used for an action that never occurred up to a certain point of time in the past.
◦ Example: Before moving to Delhi, she had never been to a big city.

• "Been to" is the correct fixed phrase (go/been to a place); with "had never" it correctly becomes "had never been to school".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "never gone" is incorrect because it lacks the auxiliary "had"; "gone" cannot stand alone as a main verb without an auxiliary.

• Option 2: "went never" is incorrect because of the wrong word order; "never" must come before the verb, not after, and "went" (Simple Past) cannot combine with "never" this way in this structure.

• Option 4: "ever been" is incorrect because it lacks the auxiliary "had", and the sentence needs the negative sense ("never"), not "ever", to state that the action did not happen.

NOTE

• "Been to" vs "gone to": "has/have/had been to" implies the person went and has already returned; "has/have/had gone to" implies the person went and has not returned.

• "Never" is normally placed immediately after the auxiliary verb: had + never + V3.

question: Select the sentence that contains no spelling errors.
option_1: The childrens playing in the kindergarden allmost broke the window of the principal's car.
option_2: The children playing in the kindergarten almost broke the window of the principal's car.
option_3: The childrens playing in the kindergarten almost broke the window of the principal's car.
option_4: The children playing in the kindergarden allmost broke the window of the principle's car.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The children playing in the kindergarten almost broke the window of the principal's car.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spellings involved are: "children" (not "childrens" — "children" is already the plural of "child", so no extra "s" is added), "kindergarten" (not "kindergarden"), "almost" (not "allmost"), and "principal's" (the head of a school, not "principle's", which means a fundamental rule or belief).

• Option 2 is the only sentence that uses all four words correctly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect: it wrongly writes "childrens" (an irregular plural should never take "-s") and "kindergarden" and "allmost".

• Option 3 is incorrect: it wrongly writes "childrens", even though "kindergarten", "almost" and "principal's" are correctly spelt here.

• Option 4 is incorrect: it wrongly writes "kindergarden" and "allmost", and confuses "principal's" (head of an institution) with "principle's" (a rule/doctrine).

NOTE

• Principal (noun/adjective: head of a school; main/chief) vs Principle (noun: a fundamental truth or rule) is a very commonly tested confusable pair.

• "Children" is one of the few irregular English plurals (child → children) that never takes an additional "-s".

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
She is in an hurry to meet her brother.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. an hurry.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the phrase "an hurry"; the correct form is "a hurry".

• Rule — Use of "a" and "an": The article "an" is used before words that begin with a vowel sound, while "a" is used before words that begin with a consonant sound. Since "hurry" begins with the consonant sound /h/ (the "h" is pronounced/aspirated), it must take "a", not "an".
◦ Example: She finished her breakfast in a hurry.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "to meet" is grammatically correct; it is the infinitive correctly used after "hurry" to show purpose.

• Option 2: "She is in" is grammatically correct; it is a correctly formed subject + verb + preposition sequence.

• Option 3: "her brother" is grammatically correct; it is a correctly formed possessive adjective + noun object.

NOTE

• The choice between "a" and "an" depends on the sound, not the spelling, of the following word — e.g., "an hour" (silent "h") but "a hurry", "a house", "a horse" (pronounced "h").

• Similarly, "a university", "a European" take "a" (consonant /y/ sound) despite starting with a vowel letter, while "an MBA", "an heir" take "an".

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blanks.
Soon after the doctor gave her the next ______ of the medicine, the patient began to ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. dose, doze.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Dose" is a noun meaning a measured quantity of a medicine to be taken at one time.
◦ Example: The doctor prescribed the next dose of the medicine after every six hours.

• "Doze" is a verb meaning to sleep lightly or briefly; to nap.
◦ Example: After taking the medicine, the patient began to doze off.

• In the sentence, the first blank needs a noun after "the next ______ of the medicine" — this must be "dose"; the second blank needs a verb after "began to ______" — this must be "doze".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "dose, dozed" is incorrect because the second blank needs the base form "doze" after "began to", not the past tense "dozed".

• Option 2: "dosed, doze" is incorrect because the first blank needs the noun "dose" (a quantity of medicine), not the verb form "dosed" (administered a dose).

• Option 4: "doze, dose" is incorrect because the two words have been interchanged — "doze" (to nap) cannot describe a quantity of medicine, and "dose" (a noun) cannot describe the act of falling into light sleep.

NOTE

• "Dose" and "doze" are commonly confused homophone-like word pairs frequently tested by SSC; always check whether the sentence needs a noun (dose = quantity) or a verb (doze = light sleep).

• Other similarly confused pairs: loose/lose, quite/quiet, breath/breathe, desert/dessert.

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A. In Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Anglican, Oriental Orthodox and Lutheran teaching, all of their faithful departed in heaven are considered saints, although some are deemed deserving of more praise or emulation.
B. In religious belief, a saint is a person who is viewed as possessing an uncommon degree of holiness, similarity, or proximity to God.
C. The term saint, however, is used differently depending on the setting and denomination.
D. Some saints receive official ecclesiastical recognition and, as a result, a public cult of veneration through the process of canonisation in the Catholic Church or glorification in the Eastern Orthodox Church.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. BCAD.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence B must open the paragraph, as it introduces the topic in general terms — "a saint is a person who is viewed as possessing..." — a definition that any coherent paragraph on this topic must begin with.

• Sentence C logically follows B: the connector "however" signals a contrast with the general definition just given, introducing the idea that the term is applied differently across denominations.

• Sentence A follows C by giving the concrete illustration of that "different usage" — listing the specific denominations (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Anglican, etc.) and how each treats sainthood.

• Sentence D logically comes last, adding further specific detail ("Some saints receive official ecclesiastical recognition...") that builds on and narrows down the idea just discussed in A.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1 (BCAD).

Additional Information

• Option 2 (BCDA) is incorrect because D (which discusses "some saints" receiving formal recognition) must follow, not precede, sentence A, which sets up the different denominational contexts to which D's detail applies.

• Option 3 (CBDA) is incorrect because it opens with C ("the term saint, however...") before the term "saint" has even been defined by B, making the contrast in C meaningless at the start.

• Option 4 (BDAC) is incorrect because it places D immediately after B, before the paragraph has explained (via C and A) that the term is used differently across denominations, breaking the logical flow.

NOTE

• In para-jumble questions, always look for the sentence that gives a general definition or introduction — it usually opens the paragraph — and for connector words like "however", "therefore", "thus", "as a result" which reveal the logical sequence.

• A sentence beginning with "Some..." (like D here) typically follows a sentence that has already set up the general category it is a subset of.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the highlighted word in the given sentence.
A strong man is a mediator between divine and mortal fate.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Lethal.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In the given sentence, "mortal" is used in the sense of deadly, fatal, or causing death — as in "mortal fate" (a fate involving death/destruction, contrasted with the "divine", i.e., immortal/godly, side). (घातक / प्राणघातक)

• "Lethal" means capable of causing death; deadly, which matches this sense of "mortal" most closely among the given options.
◦ Example: The soldiers were exposed to a lethal dose of radiation.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Delightful" means highly pleasing or charming — the opposite mood to "mortal/fatal", so it cannot be a synonym.

• Option 2: "Sincere" means honest and genuine in feeling; it has no connection with death or fatality.

• Option 3: "Overjoyed" means extremely happy; it is unrelated in meaning to "mortal".

NOTE

• "Mortal" has two common senses: (i) subject to death; human (as opposed to immortal/divine) — e.g., "all mortal beings"; and (ii) causing death; fatal — e.g., "a mortal wound", "mortal danger". Exam questions often test the second, deadlier sense, with synonyms like fatal, deadly, lethal.

• Related words: mortality (noun: the state of being mortal / death rate), immortal (antonym: living forever).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
One may accomplish many things by a little effort.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Miss.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Accomplish" means to achieve or complete something successfully. (सफलतापूर्वक पूरा करना / प्राप्त करना)

• "Miss", in the sense of to fail to achieve, reach, attain, or hit something, is the opposite of successfully accomplishing it, making it the best available antonym among the options.
◦ Example: Despite trying hard, he missed his target for the month.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Qualify" means to become eligible or officially entitled to something; it does not express failure to achieve.

• Option 2: "Retain" means to keep or continue to hold something; it is unrelated to the idea of achieving or failing to achieve a goal.

• Option 3: "Execute" means to carry out or put into effect (a plan, task, order), which is actually closer to a synonym of "accomplish" than an antonym.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "accomplish": achieve, attain, complete, fulfil, execute.

• Antonyms of "accomplish": fail, miss, abandon, forfeit.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
The farmers are harvesting the crops.
option_1: The crops are harvested by farmers.
option_2: The crops have been harvested by the farmers.
option_3: The crops are been harvested by the farmers.
option_4: The crops are being harvested by the farmers.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The crops are being harvested by the farmers.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "The farmers are harvesting the crops" is in the Active Voice, Present Continuous Tense.

• Rule — Present Continuous Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + is/am/are + V1 + ing + Object
◦ Passive: Object + is/am/are + being + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the crops" becomes the subject; since it is plural, the auxiliary "are" is used, followed by "being" and the past participle "harvested"; the original subject "the farmers" becomes the agent with "by".
◦ Passive: The crops are being harvested by the farmers.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "are harvested" (without "being") is the passive of the Simple Present Tense, not the Present Continuous.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "have been harvested" is the passive of the Present Perfect Tense.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "are been harvested" is an ungrammatical construction — "been" cannot directly follow "are" in this way; the correct continuous passive form requires "being", not "been".

NOTE

• The Present Continuous passive always uses the structure is/am/are + being + V3; forgetting "being" (as in Option 1) or wrongly using "been" instead of "being" (as in Option 3) are the two most common errors tested by SSC.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
There is a charm on the midnight air which all cannot experience.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. in the midnight air.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct preposition to use with reference to a quality or charm that exists within or is diffused through the atmosphere at a particular time is "in", giving the idiomatic and grammatically correct phrase "in the midnight air".
◦ Example: There was a strange stillness in the midnight air.

• "In" is used to describe something present or pervading within a medium (air, water, atmosphere), which is the correct sense intended here — the charm exists within the midnight air itself.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "over the midnight air" is incorrect because "over" suggests a position above something, not a quality existing within the air.

• Option 2: "around the midnight air" is incorrect because "around" suggests surrounding something from outside, which does not fit the intended meaning of a charm pervading the air.

• Option 4: "under the midnight air" is incorrect because "under" suggests a position beneath something, which is not the intended sense of the sentence.

NOTE

• Preposition-substitution questions rely on idiomatic usage rather than strict logic — "in the air" (as in "there's a feeling in the air") is a fixed, commonly used expression in English for something pervading the atmosphere.

• Other fixed prepositional phrases: "in the dark", "in the rain", "in the sun".

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
The professor's lectures are very conventional and so tedious.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Interesting.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Tedious" means long, slow, and boring; tiresome because of its dullness. (उबाऊ / थकाऊ)

• "Interesting" means arousing curiosity or attention; engaging, which is the direct opposite of "tedious".
◦ Example: The lecture, though long, was surprisingly interesting.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Informative" means providing useful information; a lecture can be informative and still be tedious, so it is not a true opposite.

• Option 3: "Idle" means not active or in use; it describes inactivity, not the quality of being engaging, so it is not the antonym of "tedious".

• Option 4: "Boring" is actually a synonym of "tedious", not its antonym, so it is incorrect.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "tedious": boring, monotonous, dull, wearisome, tiresome.

• Antonyms of "tedious": interesting, engaging, exciting, stimulating.

question:
Select the option that can substitute the underlined segment with the correct idiom.
After finishing this assignment, the employees make it a day.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. call it a day.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct idiom is "call it a day", which means to stop doing something (usually work) for the rest of the day, deciding one has done enough. (दिन भर का काम यहीं समाप्त करना)
◦ Example: After working for ten hours straight, the team decided to call it a day.

• The given sentence uses the non-idiomatic phrase "make it a day", which must be replaced with the correct, established idiom "call it a day".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "consider it a day" is not a recognised English idiom.

• Option 3: "stop it a day" is not a recognised English idiom and is grammatically awkward.

• Option 4: "ring it a day" is not a recognised English idiom (though "ring off" and "ring the curtain down on something" are separate, unrelated idioms).

NOTE

• Related idiom: "call it a night" — to stop an activity and go to bed/end the evening.

• Other common "stop/end" idioms tested by SSC: "wrap up" (to finish/conclude), "draw to a close", "bring the curtain down".

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A. Android began in 2003 as a project of the American technology company Android Inc., to develop an operating system for digital cameras.
B. In 2004, the project changed to become an operating system for smartphones.
C. Android is an operating system for cellular telephones and tablet computers.
D. In 2005, Android Inc. was bought by the American search engine company Google Inc. that transformed the OS into what it is today.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. CABD.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence C must open the paragraph as it gives the general introduction/definition of the topic — "Android is an operating system for cellular telephones and tablet computers" — before any historical detail is given.

• Sentence A logically follows, beginning the chronological account with the earliest date, 2003, describing how Android began.

• Sentence B follows next, continuing the chronology with 2004, describing the project's shift in purpose.

• Sentence D comes last, continuing the chronology with 2005, describing Google's acquisition and the OS's final transformation — a fitting concluding statement.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1 (CABD).

Additional Information

• Option 2 (ABDC) is incorrect because it opens directly with historical detail (A) before the general introduction (C) has been given, and places C, a general definition, awkwardly at the end.

• Option 3 (DCAB) is incorrect because it starts with the final chronological event (2005, D) before introducing the topic or narrating the earlier events (2003, 2004).

• Option 4 (BADC) is incorrect because it disrupts the chronological order, placing 2004 (B) before 2003 (A).

NOTE

• In para-jumbles built around a timeline, arrange sentences by their chronological markers (here, 2003 → 2004 → 2005) once the general introductory sentence has been identified.

• The sentence that offers a broad, general definition of the topic (without a specific date) is almost always the opening sentence of such a paragraph.

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A. India has an upbeat vision of a liberal, nonviolent, relatively pluralistic democracy with non-threatening global leadership.
B. Epics from mythologies like the Mahabharata and Ramayana are likened to classic Greek works like the Odyssey and Iliad and between 1 and 1000 AD, India was lauded as the 'Golden Bird' for its GDP, which was higher than China at the time.
C. Luminaries like Mahatma Gandhi and Rabindranath Tagore, as well as the arts of literature, music, dance, the software industry, Ayurveda, etc., generate a staggering array of soft power assets that highlight India's appeal to the world's population.
D. With Ashoka, Buddha, and Gandhi serving as the primary leaders, Indians are known for their core values of respect, harmony, and fraternity.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. ACDB.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence A must open the paragraph, as it presents India's overall, general self-image — "India has an upbeat vision of a liberal, nonviolent, relatively pluralistic democracy..." — the broad theme that the rest of the paragraph goes on to substantiate.

• Sentence C logically follows A, expanding on that vision by listing India's soft power assets — its luminaries (Gandhi, Tagore) and cultural strengths — that support the "appeal to the world's population" mentioned.

• Sentence D follows C, continuing to name further leadership figures (Ashoka, Buddha, and Gandhi) and linking them to India's core values, building on the idea of eminent Indian figures introduced in C.

• Sentence B comes last, adding a further historical illustration (the epics, and India's ancient GDP standing as the 'Golden Bird') that rounds off the paragraph's case for India's soft power and global standing.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1 (ACDB).

Additional Information

• Option 2 (CBAD) is incorrect because it opens with C (specific examples of soft power) before A has established the general theme those examples are meant to support.

• Option 3 (ABDC) is incorrect because it separates B (a historical/epic illustration) from its natural concluding position, disrupting the logical build-up from general vision to specific illustrative details.

• Option 4 (BCDA) is incorrect because it opens with a specific historical detail (B) rather than the general introductory statement (A), leaving the paragraph without a proper opening context.

NOTE

• In para-jumbles, the sentence that states a broad, general claim or theme (here, India's overall global vision) almost always opens the paragraph, with sentences offering specific supporting examples, names, and illustrations following in a logically connected sequence.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

We know infinitely (1)_________ about the wealthy people of Egypt than we do about the ordinary people, as most monuments were made for the rich. Houses in which ordinary Egyptian lived have not been preserved, and when most people died they were (2)_________ in simple graves. Most of our traditional sources of information (3)_________ the Old Kingdom are monuments of the rich (4)_________ pyramids and tombs. Even papyri come mainly from pyramid temples. (5) _________ this does not mean that death was the Egyptians' only preoccupation.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. more.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank is followed by the comparative conjunction "than" ("...than we do about the ordinary people"), which requires a comparative form to complete the comparison.

• "More" is the comparative form used with uncountable/abstract nouns (here, an implied "information/detail") and correctly pairs with "than" to form the structure "more...than".
◦ Example: We know more about ancient Rome than about ancient Britain.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "most" is the superlative form, used to compare three or more things without "than" (e.g., "the most information"); it cannot correctly precede "than".

• Option 3: "much" is used to indicate a large quantity in a positive statement or with "so/too" (e.g., "we know much about..."), but on its own it cannot correctly combine with "than" in this comparative structure without becoming "much more".

• Option 4: "many" is used with countable nouns (e.g., "many people"), not with the abstract, uncountable idea of "knowledge/information" being compared here.

NOTE

• Comparative structures always follow the pattern: more/-er + than, while superlative structures follow the most/-est (without "than").

• "Much" and "many" are quantifiers for uncountable and countable nouns respectively, but neither directly forms a comparison with "than" without adding "-er" or "more".

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

We know infinitely (1)_________ about the wealthy people of Egypt than we do about the ordinary people, as most monuments were made for the rich. Houses in which ordinary Egyptian lived have not been preserved, and when most people died they were (2)_________ in simple graves. Most of our traditional sources of information (3)_________ the Old Kingdom are monuments of the rich (4)_________ pyramids and tombs. Even papyri come mainly from pyramid temples. (5) _________ this does not mean that death was the Egyptians' only preoccupation.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. buried.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes what happened to ordinary people "when most people died" — a completed action in the Simple Past Tense, and since the people are the receiver of the action (they did not bury themselves), the sentence needs the Passive Voice.

• Rule — Simple Past Passive: Subject + was/were + V3. Here, the plural subject "they" requires "were", followed by the past participle "buried" (V3 of "bury").
◦ Example: They were buried in simple graves.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "buries" is a Simple Present, third-person singular form; it does not fit the past passive structure "were ______" and does not agree with the plural subject.

• Option 3: "burying" is the present participle (-ing form); it would require an auxiliary like "were being", not "were" alone, and would express a continuous, not simple, past action.

• Option 4: "bury" is the base form; it cannot directly follow "were" to form a grammatically correct passive verb phrase.

NOTE

• The passive of the Simple Past Tense always uses was/were + V3 (past participle), never the base form or the -s form.

• V1-V2-V3 of "bury": bury – buried – buried.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

We know infinitely (1)_________ about the wealthy people of Egypt than we do about the ordinary people, as most monuments were made for the rich. Houses in which ordinary Egyptian lived have not been preserved, and when most people died they were (2)_________ in simple graves. Most of our traditional sources of information (3)_________ the Old Kingdom are monuments of the rich (4)_________ pyramids and tombs. Even papyri come mainly from pyramid temples. (5) _________ this does not mean that death was the Egyptians' only preoccupation.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. about.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase needed is "sources of information about [a topic]", where the preposition "about" correctly indicates the subject matter or topic that the information concerns.
◦ Example: This book is an important source of information about ancient Egypt.

• "About" is the standard preposition used with "information" to introduce the topic being described.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "on", while sometimes used with "information" (information on a subject), is less natural here and is not the option marked correct; in this context "about" is the intended, more general and idiomatic choice.

• Option 2: "off" does not fit at all — "off" indicates separation or removal, not a topic of information.

• Option 4: "at" indicates a point in space or time, not the subject matter of information, and cannot correctly follow "sources of information".

NOTE

• Prepositions with "information": information about/on a topic; information from a source; information for a purpose.

• Preposition usage is largely idiomatic in English and must be learnt through fixed collocations rather than logical rules alone.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

We know infinitely (1)_________ about the wealthy people of Egypt than we do about the ordinary people, as most monuments were made for the rich. Houses in which ordinary Egyptian lived have not been preserved, and when most people died they were (2)_________ in simple graves. Most of our traditional sources of information (3)_________ the Old Kingdom are monuments of the rich (4)_________ pyramids and tombs. Even papyri come mainly from pyramid temples. (5) _________ this does not mean that death was the Egyptians' only preoccupation.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. like.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank introduces specific examples of the "monuments of the rich" already mentioned — namely, "pyramids and tombs". To introduce examples of a category just named, the preposition "like" (meaning "such as") is used.
◦ Example: Monuments of the rich, like pyramids and tombs, have survived for millennia.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "thus" is a conjunctive adverb meaning "as a result" or "in this way"; it introduces a consequence, not a list of examples, so it does not fit grammatically in this position.

• Option 3: "such" cannot be used alone before a noun list in this way; it would need to be paired as "such as", not "such" alone, to introduce examples.

• Option 4: "as" alone (without "such") does not correctly introduce a list of examples in this position; it would create an incomplete or awkward construction.

NOTE

• To introduce examples, English uses "like" or "such as" — both are correct, but "such" alone (without "as") is not.

• "Thus" and "as" (in the sense of "because") are used to show reason or result, not exemplification, and must not be confused with example-introducing words.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

We know infinitely (1)_________ about the wealthy people of Egypt than we do about the ordinary people, as most monuments were made for the rich. Houses in which ordinary Egyptian lived have not been preserved, and when most people died they were (2)_________ in simple graves. Most of our traditional sources of information (3)_________ the Old Kingdom are monuments of the rich (4)_________ pyramids and tombs. Even papyri come mainly from pyramid temples. (5) _________ this does not mean that death was the Egyptians' only preoccupation.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. But.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The final sentence contrasts with everything said before it: despite most surviving evidence coming from monuments of the rich and their preoccupation with death and burial, the passage clarifies that death was not the Egyptians' only concern. This is a direct contrast, which requires a contrastive conjunction.

• "But" is the most natural and commonly used coordinating conjunction to introduce such a direct contrast at the start of a sentence.
◦ Example: Most evidence comes from tombs. But this does not mean the Egyptians thought of nothing else.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Moreover" is used to add further supporting information in the same direction as what precedes it, not to contrast with it, so it does not fit here.

• Option 2: "Then" indicates a sequence in time ("next" or "after that"); it does not signal the contrast required by the sentence.

• Option 4: "Yet", while capable of showing contrast in some contexts, is not the option marked as correct here; "But" is the more direct, commonly used contrastive conjunction for this straightforward reversal of expectation.

NOTE

• Contrastive connectors: but, however, yet, nevertheless, on the other hand — used to show opposition or an unexpected turn.

• Additive connectors: moreover, furthermore, in addition, besides — used to add supporting information in the same direction as the preceding statement.
